Yesterday marked three months since I started my new position as a PhD Candidate
at the Department of Business Studies (Företagsekonomi) at Uppsala University.
Out of the five new PhD candidates that started this fall two of us are part of
the Uppsala Patent History Group ([UPHG](https://www.uphg.se)). The experience
so far has been hectic and exciting, as it often is to start any new venture.
But this is also a fitting second half to an already busy and eventful year.

During the spring it was hectic business as usual: applications to read, to
comment on and to write, ongoing projects that needed tending to, and new
projects that needed starting. I also took on the role of course coordinator for
the first time (on a course I had not taught before), and then there were a few
trips. The most important and impactful thing that happened was that I
applied for a PhD position at the department of Business Studies at Uppsala
University and got the job!

This meant that I by necessity spent most of my summer working intensely to
finish up as many of my ongoing projects as possible before going to a
conference in Daejeon and having a few weeks' vacation before attending a
two-day interdisciplinary symposium on intellectual property in Gothenburg. It
was a very exciting (pre-)start to my new role, as I will be studying
technology, relying primarily on patents. It was a very interesting event where I had the
luxury of learning from some very talented and nice people. That we happened to
meet up in beautiful Marstrand, after its busy season with perfect weather did
not hurt at all.

The next week I spent in Uppsala, getting introduced to the department, having a
kickoff and starting the first course. My life since then has been a bit of a
blur: two courses back to back, interspersed with the research school for
Management and IT's fall conference, an internal conference and a workshop. I
was supposed to attend the seventh Digital History in Sweden conference this
year, but due to a mishap on the rails south of Stockholm I arrived home around
6:00 in the morning, so I decided to sleep instead.

This brings me to last week, in which my sister PhD Candidate and I tagged along
with our supervisor to participate in a series of meetings and workshops at the
Kellogg and Wharton business schools. We not only got the chance to meet with
some very talented researchers, but also got to pitch our PhD projects and get
suggestions and comments on how to proceed (and the potential pitfalls). After
two days crammed with meetings (and a domestic flight) we managed to squeeze out
about half a day of sightseeing in Philadelphia, visiting the Liberty Bell,
eating a Cheese Steak Sandwich and visiting
[the Barnes](https://www.barnesfoundation.org/about). I am not quite sure how
representative these three points are of the city as a whole, but they were all
enjoyable.

The Barnes is full of Cézannes, Renoirs, far too few Monets, too many famous
painters for me to name or recall _and_ a cornucopia of artefacts from around
the world. One of these that caught my interest was a small Egyptian sculpture
of a slightly deformed face. So I did what any normal person would do: I took
out my phone and filmed it from as many angles as I could reasonably cover
without attracting too much attention and created a 3D model (a 3D Gaussian
Splat to be slightly more exact). During our visit, I had no idea how to do this
-- so I asked for help from an expert who pointed me towards
[Spirula Studio](https://github.com/harry7557558/spirula-studio) for generating
the initial point cloud, [SuperSplat](https://superspl.at/editor) for doing some
quick editing and a nice
[tutorial](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2nG0XgPiEmY&pp=0gcJCUYIAYcqIYzv) for
getting started.

<iframe src="../../assets/3dgs_egyptian_head_barnes.html" 
  style="width: 80%; height: 70vh; border: 0;"></iframe>

The resulting model is quite impressively close to the original. Granted, the
3DGS model would have been a lot better had I used a decent camera and perfect
lighting, and taken my time. But the surprising part is how quick it was to
generate this. Using the default settings in Spirula and some minor editing in
SuperSplat, I spent less than an hour going from having a video to this neat
little embedded model. Other than playing around with model and level editors
for videogames back in the day, I have no experience working with 3D modelling
of any kind. Those with training and experience can probably tell, but I am
still happy with the results.

On a related note, in the UPHG team we have started working more with the images
from patents, chiefly as a dimension for identifying patent families across
international borders. But this little experiment with the Egyptian head raises
my hope that it will soon be possible to generate 3D models of the patented
inventions using these drawings and diagrams from the patents. I am not quite
sure what the scientific value would be, other than that it would be extremely
cool!
